What makes hardware good for an LLM?

An accelerator should be evaluated as part of an execution system: chip, memory, interconnect, runtime, model representation, and workload. A fast matrix engine can wait on weights; a large memory can hold a model but feed it slowly; a powerful server can miss interactive latency targets while reporting excellent aggregate throughput.

This guide compares major GPU, custom accelerator, SRAM-centric, desktop, and embedded families using primary specifications and published measurements. The snapshot is 25 September 2026. Current specifications are included alongside historical landmarks. Announced capabilities and measured benchmark results are labeled separately. No hardware experiments were run for this guide.

Reading map: the problem is to supply useful arithmetic

The central hardware problem is feeding a limited set of arithmetic units with the right operands, at the right precision and time, while satisfying a capacity, latency, energy and cost constraint. This is more specific than making matrix multiplication fast. A modern LLM repeatedly changes its hardware demand: prompt processing offers long matrices; decode offers narrow matrices and growing KV reads; MoE offers a changing collection of small expert matrices; sampling and normalization introduce reductions; serving adds queues and irregular request lifetimes. A design optimized for one of these can be weak on another.

A useful objective is consequently a constrained optimization rather than a chip ranking. For a fixed quality target, minimize cost or energy while satisfying memory residency and request latency. Training replaces request latency with time to a target loss, checkpoint/restart costs and scaling efficiency. The same accelerator can occupy different places on those Pareto frontiers. The professional question is which resource constraint is active and whether a proposed architectural change relaxes it.

Read the guide in three passes. First derive the workload and roofline; do not start with the product table. Next follow the architectural landmarks: systolic inference, memory-aware exact attention, topology-aware supercomputers, asynchronous kernels and mixed precision. Finally examine present devices and measured results using that framework. The paper figures below are original crops with local PDFs; the interpretation explains which arrow, axis or scheduling choice establishes the contribution.

Five recurring design decisions

DecisionBenefit soughtCost transferred elsewhere
Bigger matrix arraysMore operations per issued instruction and operand reuseSmall/irregular matrices waste lanes; fill/drain and padding overhead
More SRAMReuse intermediate values close to arithmeticArea and leakage; storage distributed across blocks is not one uniform memory
Wider/faster external memoryFaster weights and KV deliveryPackaging, pins, HBM stack cost and power
Lower precisionFewer bytes and more multiplies per areaScaling, accumulation, conversion and accuracy management
More tightly connected devicesMore capacity and parallel arithmeticCollective startup, network contention, placement and failure domains

A later paper usually changes one of these balances after another resource improves. FlashAttention-4 is a useful example: faster tensor cores make exponentiation and shared-memory traffic more visible. Hardware progress does not remove the need for algorithm work; it changes which algorithm work has value. [36]

A common language for specifications

MetricMeaningFrequent comparison error
FLOP/s or TOPSOperations per second under a stated datatype and instructionComparing sparse FP4 with dense BF16, or counting a MAC differently
Memory capacityBytes available in a particular memory tierTreating shared system RAM as fully available device memory
Memory bandwidthMaximum or measured transfer rate to that tierComparing aggregate SRAM bandwidth with one HBM interface
Interconnect bandwidthDevice, link, direction, or system aggregate rateAdding both directions and comparing with one-way throughput
PowerTDP, board power, system power, or measured energyDividing tokens/s by TDP and calling it measured efficiency
ThroughputWork completed per timeConfusing total tokens/s with tokens/s per user
LatencyTTFT, time per output token, or request completionOmitting queueing, prefill, or tail percentiles

A multiply-add is usually counted as two floating-point operations. Structured sparsity can advertise twice the dense arithmetic rate if the supported pattern is present. Sparse MoE activation is a different kind of sparsity; top-k routing does not automatically make expert matrices compatible with 2:4 tensor-core sparsity.

Use decimal GB/s and TB/s for bandwidth unless stated otherwise. GiB is 2³⁰ bytes; GB is 10⁹ bytes. Vendor capacity conventions are not perfectly consistent, so the tables preserve source units and identify exact variants.

Derive the bottleneck before reading a leaderboard

The roofline model bounds achievable performance using arithmetic intensity I, effective memory bandwidth β, and effective arithmetic rate C. It is a lower-bound model for time; it does not include every overhead. [1]

I=FLOPsbytes moved,Cattainable≤min⁡(C,βI),T≥max⁡ ⁣(FLOPsC,bytesβ).Dense decode:Bweights≈Nb8,Fmatrix≈2NB,Iweight≈16Bb  FLOP/byte.\begin{aligned}I&=\frac{\text{FLOPs}}{\text{bytes moved}},\\C_{\mathrm{attainable}}&\le\min(C,\beta I),\\T&\ge\max\!\left(\frac{\text{FLOPs}}C,\frac{\text{bytes}}\beta\right).\\[6pt]\text{Dense decode:}\quad B_{\mathrm{weights}}&\approx\frac{Nb}{8},\\F_{\mathrm{matrix}}&\approx2NB,\\I_{\mathrm{weight}}&\approx\frac{16B}{b}\;\mathrm{FLOP/byte}.\end{aligned}ICattainable​TDense decode:Bweights​Fmatrix​Iweight​​=bytes movedFLOPs​,≤min(C,βI),≥max(CFLOPs​,βbytes​).≈8Nb​,≈2NB,≈b16B​FLOP/byte.​

At batch one, an 8B model stored at an effective 4.5 bits needs approximately 4.5 GB of weight reads per step if weights are streamed once. At 273 GB/s the ideal weight-only ceiling is about 60.7 tokens/s. At 614 GB/s it is 136.4 tokens/s. These are derived upper bounds, assuming the model fits and all bandwidth is useful; they are not measurements of Thor or M5 Max. Quantization kernels, attention, scales, and launches lower the result.

Batching amortizes weight reads across tokens, raising arithmetic intensity. Long contexts add KV reads that are not amortized in the same way across unrelated requests. Prefill usually offers larger matrix operations, while decode has narrower matrices. A hardware choice can therefore reverse between long-prompt processing and single-stream generation.

Analytical roofline illustration, not a benchmark. Supply achievable rather than peak rates for a less optimistic estimate. Dense weight-dominated model only.

FlashAttention illustrates algorithm-hardware co-design: tile attention into fast on-chip memory and avoid writing the full score matrix to HBM. It preserves exact attention in the mathematical algorithm while changing IO complexity; higher peak FLOPs alone cannot supply this saving. [32]

Foundations in depth: three rooflines and a capacity discontinuity

Start with an actual matrix shape

Let a linear layer compute C=AB where A has shape M×K and B has shape K×N. A single ideal pass performs 2MKN FLOPs. If all tensors are read/written once at widths a, b and c bytes, the compulsory transfer lower bound is MK·a + KN·b + MN·c. Real traffic is larger when tiles reload operands, padding is required, cache reuse fails or conversions spill intermediate buffers.

Iideal=2MKNMKa+KNb+MNc,M=Bbatch:Iweight≈2Mbweight,bytes=16Mbweight,bits,Iridge=Cpeakβmemory,B∗≈bweight,bits16Cpeakβmemory.\begin{aligned}I_{\mathrm{ideal}}&=\frac{2MKN}{MKa+KNb+MNc},\\M=B_{\mathrm{batch}}:\quad I_{\mathrm{weight}}&\approx\frac{2M}{b_{\mathrm{weight,bytes}}}=\frac{16M}{b_{\mathrm{weight,bits}}},\\I_{\mathrm{ridge}}&=\frac{C_{\mathrm{peak}}}{\beta_{\mathrm{memory}}},\\B^*&\approx\frac{b_{\mathrm{weight,bits}}}{16}\frac{C_{\mathrm{peak}}}{\beta_{\mathrm{memory}}}.\end{aligned}Iideal​M=Bbatch​:Iweight​Iridge​B∗​=MKa+KNb+MNc2MKN​,≈bweight,bytes​2M​=bweight,bits​16M​,=βmemory​Cpeak​​,≈16bweight,bits​​βmemory​Cpeak​​.​

The crossover formula uses the arithmetic rate of the actual instruction path. Using an FP4 peak for a weight-only INT4 kernel that dequantizes into BF16 is wrong: it may save memory traffic while still executing BF16 tensor instructions. Similarly, a low-rank adapter adds small GEMMs with their own efficiency, not a negligible fixed percentage of the base model.

For an illustrative accelerator with 1 PFLOP/s supported matrix arithmetic and 4 TB/s usable memory bandwidth, the ridge is 250 FLOP/byte. With BF16 weights, the ideal weight-only crossover occurs near batch 250; with four-bit weights it is near 62.5 if the same arithmetic peak applies. Changing precision can move the workload from bandwidth limitation to kernel or compute limitation. These values are a derivation, not a recommended batch size: KV traffic and latency constraints may prevent reaching them.

Derivation: the finite-matrix ridge and when batching cannot reach it

Assumptions and notation. Consider one dense layer Y=XW with X of shape B×K and W of shape K×N. B is the number of token rows processed together, not the number of requests over the whole run. Let a,w,c be bytes per activation, weight and output element; let F be the sustained arithmetic ceiling of the executed instruction path and β the available HBM bandwidth. Count one multiplication and one addition as two FLOPs. Assume each operand is fetched once and the output is written once. This is a compulsory-traffic lower bound, not a claim that a real kernel achieves perfect reuse. Roofline supplies the modeling framework.

1. Count work and traffic separately. There are BN output entries, each with a K-term dot product, so work is 2BKN FLOPs. The weight matrix costs KNw bytes once, but inputs and outputs cost B(Ka+Nc) bytes. Define W₀=KNw and d=Ka+Nc; d has units bytes per token row.

F(B)=2BKN,D(B)=W0+Bd,I(B)=2BKNW0+Bd  FLOP/byte,T(B)≥max⁡ ⁣(2BKNF,W0+Bdβ).\begin{aligned}F(B)&=2BKN,\\D(B)&=W_0+Bd,\\I(B)&=\frac{2BKN}{W_0+Bd}\;\mathrm{FLOP/byte},\\T(B)&\ge\max\!\left(\frac{2BKN}{F},\frac{W_0+Bd}{\beta}\right).\end{aligned}F(B)D(B)I(B)T(B)​=2BKN,=W0​+Bd,=W0​+Bd2BKN​FLOP/byte,≥max(F2BKN​,βW0​+Bd​).​

2. Solve the crossover rather than discarding activation traffic. The ridge intensity is r=F/β. Equating I(B) to r and collecting B gives:

2BKN=rW0+rBd,B(2KN−rd)=rW0,B∗=rW02KN−rdprovided 2KN>rd.\begin{aligned}2BKN&=rW_0+rBd,\\B(2KN-rd)&=rW_0,\\B^*&=\frac{rW_0}{2KN-rd}\quad\text{provided }2KN>rd.\end{aligned}2BKNB(2KN−rd)B∗​=rW0​+rBd,=rW0​,=2KN−rdrW0​​provided 2KN>rd.​

The familiar weight-only estimate r w/2 follows only when rd is negligible compared with 2KN. Otherwise it understates the required batch. Differentiating I(B) gives I′(B)=2KNW₀/(W₀+Bd)²>0, but the limiting intensity is finite: I(∞)=2KN/d. If r is at least this limit, no batch size reaches the compute roof under this traffic model. More batching still amortizes weights, but cannot eliminate per-token input/output bytes.

Example and limits. For K=N=4096, a=c=2 bytes, w=0.5 byte, F=200 TFLOP/s and β=2 TB/s, r=100 FLOP/byte. W₀=8,388,608 bytes and d=16,384 bytes/token. The crossover is B*=26.28, so the first integer batch on the compute side of this idealized model is 27. The weight-only estimate was 25. Real scale metadata, repeat loads and padding raise traffic; narrow-matrix inefficiency lowers F. Substitute measured rates for a predictive model rather than replacing them with a different datatype's advertised peak.

Exercise — Can batch size rescue a narrow matrix?

A hypothetical layer has K=N=128, BF16 inputs/outputs and one-byte weights. The hardware ridge is 100 FLOP/byte. Can any batch reach the compute roof? Show the limiting intensity and explain the answer.

Show worked solution

Here d=128×2+128×2=512 bytes/token and 2KN=32,768 FLOPs/token. Therefore:

I(∞)=32,768512=64  FLOP/byte<100,2KN−rd=32,768−100×512=−18,432.\begin{aligned}I(\infty)&=\frac{32{,}768}{512}=64\;\mathrm{FLOP/byte}<100,\\2KN-rd&=32{,}768-100\times512=-18{,}432.\end{aligned}I(∞)2KN−rd​=51232,768​=64FLOP/byte<100,=32,768−100×512=−18,432.​

The negative denominator means there is no positive crossover batch. Weight traffic is amortized as batch grows, but every output token still requires enough activation/output movement to keep the ideal intensity below the ridge. This conclusion uses the stated traffic model; retaining inputs/outputs in a faster cache would require a different roofline at the HBM level.

KV traffic puts a ceiling on batching benefits

For a model with P dense parameters, L layers, Hkv KV heads, query-head count Hq, head dimension d, context S, batch B and value width skv bytes, a simplified decoding step has the following costs. Weight width sw includes packing/scaling overhead if appropriate. Attention FLOPs below count QK and PV but omit softmax and projection details already partly represented in P.

Dweights≈Psw,DKV≈2LBSHkvd skv,Flinear≈2PB,Fattention≈4LBSHqd,Tstep≥max⁡ ⁣(Flinear+FattentionC,Dweights+DKVβHBM),S∗≈Psw2LBHkvd skv(traffic crossover).\begin{aligned}D_{\mathrm{weights}}&\approx Ps_w,\\D_{\mathrm{KV}}&\approx2LBSH_{\mathrm{kv}}d\,s_{\mathrm{kv}},\\F_{\mathrm{linear}}&\approx2PB,\\F_{\mathrm{attention}}&\approx4LBSH_qd,\\T_{\mathrm{step}}&\ge\max\!\left(\frac{F_{\mathrm{linear}}+F_{\mathrm{attention}}}{C},\frac{D_{\mathrm{weights}}+D_{\mathrm{KV}}}{\beta_{\mathrm{HBM}}}\right),\\S^*&\approx\frac{Ps_w}{2LBH_{\mathrm{kv}}d\,s_{\mathrm{kv}}}\quad\text{(traffic crossover).}\end{aligned}Dweights​DKV​Flinear​Fattention​Tstep​S∗​≈Psw​,≈2LBSHkv​dskv​,≈2PB,≈4LBSHq​d,≥max(CFlinear​+Fattention​​,βHBM​Dweights​+DKV​​),≈2LBHkv​dskv​Psw​​(traffic crossover).​

For the 8B, 4.5-bit example, weight bytes are 4.5 GB. With L=32, Hkv=8, d=128 and BF16 KV, each sequence adds 128 KiB of cache per context token. The traffic crossover is approximately 34,332/B context tokens. At batch one this is a long context; at batch 32 it is only about 1,073 tokens in this idealized accounting. This does not mean attention must dominate total time at that length: cache reuse, fused kernels, GQA layouts and different achieved rates matter. It means the familiar claim that each extra request is nearly free after weights are loaded has stopped being a good bandwidth model.

Grouped-query attention improves this arithmetic by sharing K/V across query heads. Its ideal KV-only intensity is roughly 2Hq/(Hkv·skv) FLOP/byte, before softmax and reuse imperfections. GQA can thus improve both capacity and bandwidth without changing query-head count. MLA changes the representation more substantially; use its latent dimensions and reconstruction path rather than plugging the original Hkv into the formula. Architecture, cache format and hardware cannot be compared independently.

Derivation: the KV asymptote, latency saturation, and a feasible batch interval

Assumptions. In one dense decoding iteration, B sequences each emit one token and have the same context S. Let W bytes be the resident weights streamed once per iteration, k bytes the K/V data read per sequence, and f FLOPs the work per sequence. Ignore overlap with another iteration, prefix sharing and output traffic for this first model. Effective weight width includes scale metadata. GQA is represented by Hkv stored heads and Hq query heads.

k=2LSHkvd sKV,f≈2P+4LSHqd,I(B)=BfW+Bk,lim⁡B→∞I(B)=fk.\begin{aligned}k&=2LSH_{\mathrm{kv}}d\,s_{\mathrm{KV}},\\f&\approx2P+4LSH_qd,\\I(B)&=\frac{Bf}{W+Bk},\\\lim_{B\to\infty}I(B)&=\frac fk.\end{aligned}kfI(B)B→∞lim​I(B)​=2LSHkv​dsKV​,≈2P+4LSHq​d,=W+BkBf​,=kf​.​

1. Derive the two consequences of per-sequence cache traffic. The numerator and KV term both scale with B, while the weight term does not. Dividing numerator and denominator by B proves the finite intensity limit. With ridge r=F/β, the exact ideal crossover is B*=rW/(f−rk), and exists only if f>rk. In a bandwidth-bound region the iteration takes approximately (W+Bk)/β, giving aggregate throughput:

R(B)=BT(B)≈βBW+Bk,lim⁡B→∞R(B)=βk,Tinter-token≈W+Bkβper request.\begin{aligned}R(B)&=\frac{B}{T(B)}\approx\frac{\beta B}{W+Bk},\\\lim_{B\to\infty}R(B)&=\frac\beta k,\\T_{\mathrm{inter\text{-}token}}&\approx\frac{W+Bk}{\beta}\quad\text{per request}.\end{aligned}R(B)B→∞lim​R(B)Tinter-token​​=T(B)B​≈W+BkβB​,=kβ​,≈βW+Bk​per request.​

Thus aggregate throughput approaches a ceiling while each request's inter-token time continues to grow. Batching trades latency for throughput; “the weights are already loaded” does not make extra sequences free.

2. Add feasibility before selecting a batch. If M bytes of HBM are usable, C₀ is non-KV workspace and kalloc is allocated KV bytes per sequence including paging/slack, then B≤floor((M−W−C₀)/kalloc). An inter-token target τ imposes B≤(βτ−W)/k in the bandwidth model. To reach the compute side, a valid integer batch must also satisfy B≥ceil(B*). The intersection can be empty because of the intensity asymptote, memory, or latency. Allocation bytes and read bytes need not be equal.

Example. With P=8×10⁹, W=4.5 GB, L=32, Hkv=8, Hq=32, d=128, S=8192 and BF16 KV, k=1,073,741,824 bytes and f≈20.295×10⁹ FLOPs per sequence. Consequently f/k≈18.90 FLOP/byte. A 250-FLOP/byte ridge cannot be reached by batching at this context under these assumptions. This is a derived workload result, not a chip benchmark. Exact KV tiling, prefix reuse and achieved attention throughput can change the relevant service times.

Exercise — Which constraint limits admission?

Use W=4.5 GB, k=kalloc=1 GiB per sequence, β=3 TB/s, M=80 GB, C₀=8 GB and a 10 ms inter-token budget. Assume the bandwidth model applies. Find the memory and latency batch limits using decimal GB/TB and binary GiB.

Show worked solution

Convert k=2³⁰=1,073,741,824 bytes. The memory budget leaves 80−4.5−8=67.5 GB for caches:

Bmemory=⌊67.5×109230⌋=62,βτ=3×1012×0.010=30×109  bytes,Blatency=⌊(30−4.5)×109230⌋=23.\begin{aligned}B_{\mathrm{memory}}&=\left\lfloor\frac{67.5\times10^9}{2^{30}}\right\rfloor=62,\\\beta\tau&=3\times10^{12}\times0.010=30\times10^9\;\mathrm{bytes},\\B_{\mathrm{latency}}&=\left\lfloor\frac{(30-4.5)\times10^9}{2^{30}}\right\rfloor=23.\end{aligned}Bmemory​βτBlatency​​=⌊23067.5×109​⌋=62,=3×1012×0.010=30×109bytes,=⌊230(30−4.5)×109​⌋=23.​

The active limit is 23 sequences. At B=23, T≈(4.5×10⁹+23×2³⁰)/(3×10¹²)=9.73 ms; B=24 requires about 10.09 ms. A scheduler should leave additional headroom for other operators and variability, so 23 is an optimistic analytical maximum, not an operational recommendation.

The relevant roof may be inside the chip

A hierarchical roofline applies separately to HBM, L2, SRAM/shared memory, register accesses and network links. An operation can be HBM-efficient and still saturate shared-memory banks. Tensor cores can wait for scalar exponentials even when all operands are resident. A more realistic resource lower bound is the maximum of resource-specific service times, plus unavoidable sequential sections.

Tkernel≥max⁡{FtensorCtensor,FscalarCscalar,Nexp⁡Cexp⁡,DHBMβHBM,Dsharedβshared,Dnetworkβnetwork}+Tserial.\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{kernel}}\ge\max\biggl\{&\frac{F_{\mathrm{tensor}}}{C_{\mathrm{tensor}}},\frac{F_{\mathrm{scalar}}}{C_{\mathrm{scalar}}},\frac{N_{\exp}}{C_{\exp}},\\&\frac{D_{\mathrm{HBM}}}{\beta_{\mathrm{HBM}}},\frac{D_{\mathrm{shared}}}{\beta_{\mathrm{shared}}},\frac{D_{\mathrm{network}}}{\beta_{\mathrm{network}}}\biggr\}+T_{\mathrm{serial}}.\end{aligned}Tkernel​≥max{​Ctensor​Ftensor​​,Cscalar​Fscalar​​,Cexp​Nexp​​,βHBM​DHBM​​,βshared​Dshared​​,βnetwork​Dnetwork​​}+Tserial​.​

This is not a claim that every cost overlaps perfectly. It provides a diagnostic: measure or model each denominator, find the largest term, then inspect dependencies that prevent overlap. An optimization that lowers a noncritical term can have no runtime effect. Conversely, adding FLOPs can reduce runtime if it removes more expensive traffic, as attention recomputation demonstrates.

Capacity is a feasibility constraint before it is a speed metric

Peak live memory is weights plus KV plus activations/workspace plus communication buffers, allocator slack and runtime state. Inference weight residency for a 70B dense model at an effective 4.5 bits is 39.375 GB, about 36.67 GiB, before any other state. It cannot fit entirely into a 32 GB card. A 48 GB card may fit weights but have little room for long contexts or high concurrency. A 128 GB unified-memory machine can fit a much larger workload while offering less bandwidth than a high-end discrete GPU.

The resulting performance curve has discontinuities. Crossing the fit threshold can eliminate PCIe offload or one distributed boundary. Below that threshold, a modest capacity difference can outweigh a large arithmetic difference; above it, an extra 20 GB may have no effect on one short request. This is why product tables must be interpreted with a concrete memory budget rather than an average “performance per GB.”

Era 1 · TPU v1 and the explicit dataflow accelerator, 2015–2017

The first TPU paper is a landmark because it describes a deployed inference accelerator and evaluates it against production latency constraints. It did not begin from the assumption that average utilization or peak throughput was the only objective. Its matrix unit, accumulators, unified activation buffer and off-chip weight memory are arranged to make predictable inference efficient. [33]

Read the diagram from the operands outward. Weights travel through a dedicated FIFO into the matrix multiply unit. Intermediate accumulations need more numerical range than individual low-precision products, so accumulators are a separate storage resource. Activations are retained in the unified buffer and processed by activation/pooling hardware before reuse or output. The floor plan makes the cost visible: the arithmetic array occupies only part of the die, while storage and data movement consume substantial area.

A systolic array passes operands between neighboring multiply-accumulate cells on a schedule. This replaces repeated long-distance fetches with local reuse. Suppose a tile computes A[M,K]B[K,N]. An element of A can be reused across N outputs and an element of B across M outputs. Keeping one operand or partial sums stationary reduces expensive accesses. The names weight-stationary, output-stationary and input-stationary describe which quantity receives that priority; actual accelerators and compilers often combine several levels of tiling.

The penalty is shape sensitivity. A square array mapped to a skinny decode matrix may leave many cells unused unless multiple requests, heads or tiles are packed together. Even a well-filled array must ramp a wavefront through the mesh and drain results. When K is short, these fixed phases are a larger fraction of execution. Therefore the number of physical MACs is an upper bound whose attainability depends on M, N, K and the scheduling interface.

The TPU v1 roofline places MLP/LSTM workloads in the sloping bandwidth region and other workloads nearer the compute ceiling. It also contains a point below the expected roof, illustrating that tensor dimensions and implementation constraints can create another limit. The lesson survives newer chips: if a workload sits on the bandwidth slope, faster multipliers change the height of a roof it cannot reach. Increasing batch size can shift the point to the right, but only while the response-time requirement permits it.

This motivates a three-part experiment for any new accelerator: measure an aligned large GEMM to establish arithmetic capability; measure the exact skinny or irregular shapes used by the model; then measure the complete latency-constrained service. The gaps identify mapping and orchestration costs. A full-service slowdown despite a fast GEMM is not contradictory evidence—it localizes the missing resource.

Era 2 · GPUs, tiling, and the FlashAttention reset, 2022

GPUs expose many execution blocks, with registers and programmer-managed shared memory close to arithmetic. An LLM kernel normally traverses HBM → cache → shared memory/registers → matrix/vector units. A naïve attention implementation writes the S×S score matrix, reads it for softmax, writes probabilities and reads them again for multiplication by V. That traffic grows quadratically even though the output and Q/K/V grow linearly in sequence length. [32]

The paper's contribution is to change the execution order so the large intermediate is never materialized in HBM. Tiling by itself is insufficient because softmax normally requires the maximum and denominator over an entire row. Online softmax supplies a compact state that merges partial blocks while maintaining numerical stability. For score block j, retain row maximum mj, exponential sum lj and an unnormalized weighted-value accumulator uj. With old state m,l,u and new scores xj, update as follows.

mnew=max⁡(m,max⁡(xj)),ρ=em−mnew,pj=exj−mnew,lnew=ρl+sum⁡(pj),unew=ρu+pjVj,O=ul.\begin{aligned}m_{\mathrm{new}}&=\max(m,\max(x_j)),\\\rho&=e^{m-m_{\mathrm{new}}},\\p_j&=e^{x_j-m_{\mathrm{new}}},\\l_{\mathrm{new}}&=\rho l+\operatorname{sum}(p_j),\\u_{\mathrm{new}}&=\rho u+p_jV_j,\\O&=\frac ul.\end{aligned}mnew​ρpj​lnew​unew​O​=max(m,max(xj​)),=em−mnew​,=exj​−mnew​,=ρl+sum(pj​),=ρu+pj​Vj​,=lu​.​

The rescaling is essential. Simply summing independently normalized block outputs gives the wrong answer because each block has a different denominator. The same merge principle later supports split-K decode kernels and distributed Ring Attention. This is a useful research-development connection: a numerically stable algebraic reformulation becomes a building block at several hardware scales.

FlashAttention also recomputes selected intermediates during backward rather than saving the whole attention matrix. Extra arithmetic can be cheaper than an HBM round trip. With a fast memory budget M measured in elements and typical dimensional assumptions, the paper derives HBM traffic scaling involving S²d²/M rather than materializing S² intermediates. This is an IO-complexity result, not elimination of exact attention's quadratic arithmetic.

The figure's runtime bars should be read as an explanation, not a universal multiplier. Several separate kernels and intermediate-memory transactions collapse into one tiled kernel. Gains depend on sequence length, head dimension, masking, dropout, dtype and baseline fusion. A modern vendor attention kernel may already use the same principle, so comparing with an unfused baseline years later would answer a different question.

Decode requires a different occupancy strategy

During prefill, many query rows create many independent work tiles. During single-token decode, query length is one; assigning work only by batch and head may launch too few threadblocks to occupy the GPU. Split-K approaches partition the history across multiple blocks, compute partial attention states, then merge them. They trade more parallelism for a reduction and temporary storage. At short contexts, that extra reduction can cost more than it saves.

FlashDecoding++ makes shape-sensitive kernel design explicit: narrow GEMMs, softmax synchronization and static dataflows each need attention. Its proposed unified-max approach has numerical handling assumptions; it should not be treated as permission to discard stable softmax arbitrarily. The broad architectural insight is durable: a prefill kernel and decode kernel can have the same mathematical expression but require different work decomposition. [37]

Derivation: why SRAM capacity sets the reuse a matrix tile can obtain

Model. A GEMM output tile has m rows and n columns and reduces over k input coordinates. Each reduction tile loads mk activation elements and kn weight elements. Let both operands use s bytes and let each live accumulator use sacc bytes. Assume one output tile remains resident while these inputs are reused. This idealization explains the dataflow in the TPU and FlashAttention discussions; bank conflicts and tensor-instruction tile constraints are added afterward. FlashAttention, TPU v1.

1. Count reuse. Each loaded activation participates in n products and each loaded weight in m products. Ignoring the output write for a sufficiently long reduction:

Ftile=2mnk,Dtile,in=s(mk+kn)=sk(m+n),Itile≈2mns(m+n).\begin{aligned}F_{\mathrm{tile}}&=2mnk,\\D_{\mathrm{tile,in}}&=s(mk+kn)=sk(m+n),\\I_{\mathrm{tile}}&\approx\frac{2mn}{s(m+n)}.\end{aligned}Ftile​Dtile,in​Itile​​=2mnk,=s(mk+kn)=sk(m+n),≈s(m+n)2mn​.​

For fixed m+n, the product mn is maximized by m=n. Writing m=n=t gives Itile≈t/s. Larger square tiles increase reuse linearly, but their accumulator area grows quadratically.

2. Impose the fast-memory budget. With two buffers for operands and one accumulator tile, a simple capacity bound is Mfast≥2sk(m+n)+sacc mn. For a square tile:

sacct2+4skt≤Mfast,t≲Mfastsaccif accumulation dominates,Itile≲1sMfastsacc.\begin{aligned}s_{\mathrm{acc}}t^2+4skt&\le M_{\mathrm{fast}},\\t&\lesssim\sqrt{\frac{M_{\mathrm{fast}}}{s_{\mathrm{acc}}}}\quad\text{if accumulation dominates},\\I_{\mathrm{tile}}&\lesssim\frac1s\sqrt{\frac{M_{\mathrm{fast}}}{s_{\mathrm{acc}}}}.\end{aligned}sacc​t2+4skttItile​​≤Mfast​,≲sacc​Mfast​​​if accumulation dominates,≲s1​sacc​Mfast​​​.​

The square-root dependence explains why doubling fast-memory capacity does not double attainable tile reuse. The exact allocation depends on whether accumulators live in registers, dedicated tensor memory, or SRAM; separate budgets must be checked if the resources cannot substitute for one another. Also, a tile can fit yet leave too few independent thread blocks to occupy the device.

Numerical illustration. Take s=2, sacc=4, k=32 and a combined illustrative budget Mfast=128 KiB. The inequality becomes 4t²+256t≤131,072. Its positive root is about 151.8. A hardware-friendly t=128 consumes 98,304 bytes and has ideal input intensity 64 FLOP/byte. t=160 consumes 143,360 bytes and violates the budget. This is why a nominally faster arithmetic array can wait for data even when HBM traffic has already been optimized.

Exercise — Does a larger tile still fit with double buffering?

In the preceding model, keep s=2, sacc=4, k=32 and Mfast=128 KiB. Compute the storage and ideal input intensity for t=144. Explain why this calculation does not prove that t=144 is a valid kernel tile.

Show worked solution
M(144)=4×1442+256×144=82,944+36,864=119,808  bytes<131,072,I≈1442=72  FLOP/byte.\begin{aligned}M(144)&=4\times144^2+256\times144\\&=82{,}944+36{,}864=119{,}808\;\mathrm{bytes}<131{,}072,\\I&\approx\frac{144}{2}=72\;\mathrm{FLOP/byte}.\end{aligned}M(144)I​=4×1442+256×144=82,944+36,864=119,808bytes<131,072,≈2144​=72FLOP/byte.​

The abstract memory model permits the tile. The actual instruction shape may require dimensions divisible by a particular tile size; register allocation may be quantized per thread; double buffers and accumulators may draw from different physical memories; occupancy or bank conflicts may worsen. The calculation supplies a necessary capacity check under its assumptions, not a complete mapping proof.

Era 3 · The interconnect becomes part of the accelerator: TPU v4, 2020–2023

TPU v4 extends the unit of design from a chip to an optically reconfigurable supercomputer. It combines matrix/vector execution with a 3D inter-chip network; optical circuit switches can reconnect portions of the machine. The distinction matters because distributed training and embedding workloads can be limited by communication and allocation even when each individual chip is fast. [34]

A 4×4×4 building block keeps short links electrical. Exposed faces connect optically to other blocks. The optical switches behave like a reconfigurable wiring arrangement: they can form suitable slices and avoid failed components. They do not inspect each tensor element and choose its mathematical destination. Collective algorithms and compiler mappings still determine which traffic follows those links.

For a d-dimensional mesh or torus, the number of links crossing a bisection grows more slowly than the number of nodes. An all-to-all workload demands many source–destination paths simultaneously, so injection bandwidth at each chip is insufficient to predict completion time. If half the devices must exchange Q bytes with the other half through total bisection bandwidth Bbisect, time is at least Q/Bbisect even if every endpoint advertises a much larger local rate. Expert routing and parameter redistribution can therefore respond strongly to topology.

The regular and twisted drawings use the same nodes but alter wraparound links. The objective is to improve path diversity and bisection for elongated slices, rather than add arithmetic. Logical tensor axes should be mapped to physical directions with this traffic pattern in mind: an axis with frequent all-reduce or all-to-all is more demanding than an axis with occasional point-to-point transfers.

For the displayed 4×4×8 case, measured all-to-all rises from 40.0 to 65.4 GB/s per TPU when using the twisted topology; for 4×8×8 it rises from 39.6 to 51.7. These are approximately 1.64× and 1.31× changes derived from the figure. They are not end-to-end model speedups. A model benefits in proportion to its exposed communication, and it may trade network efficiency against a different model-parallel partition.

The paper also separates matrix-oriented TensorCores from SparseCores for embedding work. Embedding lookup combines indexing, irregular gathers and reductions; a dense matrix array cannot automatically execute it efficiently. This is conceptually relevant to MoE, although embedding acceleration and expert GEMM acceleration are different workloads. The general lesson is that a heterogeneous workload can justify dedicated data movement and sparse-operation engines even when they contribute little to advertised FLOP/s.

Availability changes delivered performance

At thousands of chips, the probability that every component is simultaneously usable falls unless the system tolerates faults. Reconfigurable topology improves schedulable capacity by routing around unavailable parts. This is another meaning of goodput: usable work delivered over time, including fragmentation and failures. It should be distinguished from a single benchmark run on a healthy slice. Systems intended for long training runs should compare restart time, checkpoint bandwidth and allocation success, not just peak arithmetic.

Derivation: useful cluster throughput includes checkpoint and failure losses

Assumptions. A tightly synchronized job has useful progress rate R₀ while running. Failures arrive with rate λ per unit of wall time; a checkpoint costs c time, checkpoints are spaced by τ units of useful running time, and recovery costs r time per failure. Assume λτ is small, checkpoint time is short, failures are independent of progress, and the most recent checkpoint is durable. The TPU availability discussion motivates counting delivered progress rather than healthy-chip peak. The following first-order model is a derivation, not a fitted claim about that system.

1. Count checkpoint overhead. Over a long run, approximately one checkpoint is taken per τ units of useful progress, so the fraction lost to checkpointing is c/τ to first order.

2. Count lost work. Conditional on one failure within an interval and under the small-rate approximation, failure time is approximately uniform across that interval. The expected work since the last checkpoint is therefore (1/τ)∫₀^τt dt=τ/2. Each failure additionally requires r recovery time.

h(τ)≈cτ+λτ2+λr,R≈R0[1−h(τ)],h′(τ)=−cτ2+λ2=0⟹τ∗≈2cλ.\begin{aligned}h(\tau)&\approx\frac c\tau+\frac{\lambda\tau}{2}+\lambda r,\\R&\approx R_0[1-h(\tau)],\\h'(\tau)&=-\frac c{\tau^2}+\frac\lambda2=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\tau^*\approx\sqrt{\frac{2c}{\lambda}}.\end{aligned}h(τ)Rh′(τ)​≈τc​+2λτ​+λr,≈R0​[1−h(τ)],=−τ2c​+2λ​=0⟹τ∗≈λ2c​​.​

Interpretation. Frequent checkpoints reduce recomputation after failure but interrupt more progress. The recovery term changes delivered throughput but does not change this simplified optimum because it is independent of τ. For independent devices that each fail at rate λ₁ and all are required, λ≈nλ₁; scaling to more devices can shorten the optimal checkpoint interval. Redundancy and elastic recovery change that assumption.

Example and limits. With c=2 minutes and a job mean time between failures of 20 hours (λ=1/1200 per minute), τ*≈69.3 minutes. Checkpoint loss and lost-progress loss are each about 2.89%, before recovery. If failures are frequent enough that λτ is not small, or checkpointing overlaps computation while contending for IO, this approximation is inadequate. The model's point is to expose the terms that a peak-throughput comparison leaves out.

Era 4 · Hopper: overlap independent engines, 2022–2024

Hopper's asynchronous facilities expose more of the machine's internal concurrency. The Tensor Memory Accelerator can move multidimensional blocks without making every compute thread perform the address work, while warp-group matrix instructions issue matrix work asynchronously. The opportunity is to overlap load, matrix arithmetic and scalar processing; the challenge is coordinating their lifetimes without excessive registers or barriers. [41] [35]

A producer–consumer kernel assigns some warps to move operands and other warps to compute. Buffers carry epochs or phases so a consumer cannot read an unfinished tile and a producer cannot overwrite a tile still in use. Double buffering can hide a load when computation on the previous tile lasts at least as long as the transfer. Adding more buffers increases overlap opportunity but consumes shared memory and may reduce the number of resident blocks, creating a resource tradeoff.

The FlashAttention-3 schedule uses two warpgroups to interleave GEMM and softmax. Softmax depends on the output of QK, so one group cannot perform those operations for the same tile simultaneously. Another group can execute a different tile's GEMM during that interval. The timing picture therefore exploits independence across groups; it does not violate the dependency within a group. This is the same reasoning needed when deciding whether network communication can overlap a dependent computation.

Derivation: pipeline fill, steady-state overlap, and the buffers that make it possible

Setup. A kernel processes n tiles. Loading each tile takes ℓ seconds and computing on it takes c seconds. Assume independent load and compute engines, identical tiles, enough bandwidth when concurrent, and two input buffers so tile i+1 can load while tile i computes. A dependency still requires every tile to load before its own computation. This is the basic scheduling idea behind asynchronous pipelines; FlashAttention-3 adds further stages and dependencies.

1. Derive the schedule length. Without overlap, all n tiles cost n(ℓ+c). With a two-stage pipeline the first result needs ℓ+c. Each additional result is limited by the slower engine, giving:

Tserial=n(ℓ+c),Tpipeline=ℓ+c+(n−1)max⁡(ℓ,c),S=n(ℓ+c)ℓ+c+(n−1)max⁡(ℓ,c),lim⁡n→∞S=ℓ+cmax⁡(ℓ,c)≤2.\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{serial}}&=n(\ell+c),\\T_{\mathrm{pipeline}}&=\ell+c+(n-1)\max(\ell,c),\\S&=\frac{n(\ell+c)}{\ell+c+(n-1)\max(\ell,c)},\\\lim_{n\to\infty}S&=\frac{\ell+c}{\max(\ell,c)}\le2.\end{aligned}Tserial​Tpipeline​Sn→∞lim​S​=n(ℓ+c),=ℓ+c+(n−1)max(ℓ,c),=ℓ+c+(n−1)max(ℓ,c)n(ℓ+c)​,=max(ℓ,c)ℓ+c​≤2.​

The ceiling is two for these two equally necessary stages, reached only if they balance. If loading is ten times slower than computation, pipeline overlap has much less to hide. “Overlap” therefore has an amount, not just an enabled/disabled state.

2. State what breaks the model. Double buffering needs memory for two input tiles. If the same buffer is overwritten while computation still uses it, the schedule is incorrect. If load/dequantization consumes SM instructions needed by computation, concurrent ℓ and c may exceed their isolated measurements. If a tile's scale depends on a previous result, readiness rather than engine independence becomes the limiter.

Example. Ten tiles with ℓ=4 μs and c=6 μs take 100 μs serially and 4+6+9×6=64 μs when ideally pipelined: 1.5625×, below the 1.667× steady-state limit. The fill/drain cost matters for short kernels. This is why an instruction-level overlap diagram must be connected to the actual number of tiles, buffer residency and dependency chain.

Exercise — When overlap slows the individual stages

For ten tiles, isolated load/compute durations are 4 and 6 μs. Concurrent use makes them 5 and 8 μs because of contention. Find the pipelined runtime and speedup against the original serial execution. Would quoting the ideal 1.5625× still be valid?

Show worked solution
Tserial=10(4+6)=100  μs,Tconcurrent=5+8+9×8=85  μs,S=10085≈1.176×.\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{serial}}&=10(4+6)=100\;\mu\mathrm s,\\T_{\mathrm{concurrent}}&=5+8+9\times8=85\;\mu\mathrm s,\\S&=\frac{100}{85}\approx1.176\times.\end{aligned}Tserial​Tconcurrent​S​=10(4+6)=100μs,=5+8+9×8=85μs,=85100​≈1.176×.​

The ideal 64 μs estimate assumes isolated stage durations survive concurrency, which the question explicitly violates. Overlap still helps here, but only by about 15% in latency. Measure the concurrent timeline; adding isolated peak rates overstates the gain when engines compete for shared resources.

Occupancy is a means, not the target

More resident warps help hide latency, but a kernel with high occupancy can still perform redundant loads or use an inefficient matrix shape. Conversely, a carefully pipelined kernel with lower occupancy can saturate tensor cores. Registers hold accumulators and softmax state; too many live values trigger spills into slower memory or restrict occupancy. A larger tile increases reuse while increasing accumulator size. Kernel tuning must balance all three effects instead of maximizing one occupancy percentage.

The original head-dimension-256 plots separate causal and non-causal attention. Causal masking removes upper-triangular work and changes scheduling balance, so the two panels should not be averaged without a workload definition. Increasing sequence length improves available parallelism and amortizes overhead in many cases. The plotted TFLOP/s measures attention's defined arithmetic count divided by kernel time; it does not include feed-forward layers, communication, scheduler delay or model loading.

The reported FP16/BF16 and FP8 achievements are also different experiments. FP8 block quantization and incoherent processing address numerical range/outliers while using faster matrix instructions. A kernel-level numerical-error comparison does not establish unchanged downstream quality for every full model. Precision must be evaluated at the level where the application makes its quality claim.

Era 5 · Blackwell and asymmetric scaling: why faster matmul exposes softmax

FlashAttention-4 is particularly valuable hardware literature because it explains a failure mode of simplistic generational comparisons. On its B200 target, tensor-core throughput increases faster than shared-memory and exponentiation resources. A direct port of a previous high-performance attention kernel can therefore spend a larger fraction of time on non-matrix work. [36]

For a forward tile M×N with head width d, the two attention GEMMs perform 4MNd operations. The paper uses 8,192 BF16 tensor operations per clock per SM in its model. At M=N=d=128 this gives 1,024 cycles. Exponentiating MN elements at 16 operations/clock also requires 1,024 cycles. Doubling M doubles both demands. The original table shows shared-memory times of 768 and 1,536 cycles for the two tile configurations, below the corresponding tensor/exp limits in these forward cases.

The correct conclusion is not that shared memory always dominates Blackwell attention. The binding resource depends on the forward/backward graph and tile. Backward uses five matrix products and additional intermediate traffic; the paper's backward analysis finds shared-memory pressure more restrictive. Distinguishing those graphs avoids turning a case-specific observation into an architecture slogan.

Tensor memory (TMEM) lets matrix operations write accumulators into a dedicated storage level, reducing pressure on the normal register file. The staggered pipeline processes high and low query tiles so exponentiation and matrix work remain useful concurrently. Polynomial-based exponential emulation redistributes work toward ordinary arithmetic units; conditional rescaling skips work when numerical conditions permit it. These are changes to resource demand, not merely launch-parameter tuning.

The two-CTA mode lets a pair of blocks cooperate on a larger matrix operation. Sharing operands reduces redundant staging; coordinated access to distributed shared memory also helps restructure backward reductions. That benefit comes with placement and lifetime constraints: the paired blocks must exist together and use a compatible execution mode. A compiler or kernel that ignores these constraints cannot obtain the feature's theoretical gain.

Derivation: a faster tensor core can expose another roof without speeding the model proportionally

Separate two models. Amdahl's law concerns serially accumulated elapsed-time fractions. A resource roofline concerns work that may overlap and is bounded by a maximum. Using a sum where there is overlap double-counts time; using a maximum for dependent stages hides real serial work. The asymmetric resource discussion in FlashAttention-4 is best understood through both models.

1. Amdahl's law from elapsed time. Let baseline time T consist of an improvable fraction fT and an unchanged fraction (1−f)T. Speeding only the former by s gives:

Tnew=(1−f)T+fTs,S=TTnew=1(1−f)+f/s,lim⁡s→∞S=11−f.\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{new}}&=(1-f)T+\frac{fT}{s},\\S&=\frac{T}{T_{\mathrm{new}}}=\frac1{(1-f)+f/s},\\\lim_{s\to\infty}S&=\frac1{1-f}.\end{aligned}Tnew​Ss→∞lim​S​=(1−f)T+sfT​,=Tnew​T​=(1−f)+f/s1​,=1−f1​.​

For f=0.8 and s=4, the end-to-end gain is 1/(0.2+0.2)=2.5×. This formula assumes the categories remain disjoint and the optimization does not change other work, batching or communication.

2. The critical resource can switch. Suppose one kernel has 10 μs unavoidable serial work and ideal overlapping service times of 40 μs tensor work, 30 μs shared-memory work and 12 μs scalar work. Its modeled time is 10+max(40,30,12)=50 μs. Doubling the tensor rate changes that to 10+max(20,30,12)=40 μs, only 1.25×. The tensor core is no longer the limiter; further tensor-only acceleration has no benefit in this bound.

3. Interpret the hardware claim. More FLOP/s helps only the portion of execution that actually uses those instructions and remains limited by them. Reduced precision may also change transfer bytes, scaling work and accuracy, so it can move several terms simultaneously. Measure those effects rather than assigning the arithmetic peak ratio to a whole model. The argument also explains why spending extra scalar instructions to reduce HBM traffic can make a kernel faster.

Use the kernel example above. After tensor time is reduced to 20 μs, compare (A) reducing it again to 10 μs and (B) reducing shared-memory time from 30 to 18 μs. Keep serial=10 and scalar=12 μs. Compute both runtimes and gains over the original 50 μs.

A:T=10+max⁡(10,30,12)=40  μs,S=5040=1.25×,B:T=10+max⁡(20,18,12)=30  μs,S=5030≈1.667×.\begin{aligned}\text{A:}\quad T&=10+\max(10,30,12)=40\;\mu\mathrm s,&S&=\frac{50}{40}=1.25\times,\\\text{B:}\quad T&=10+\max(20,18,12)=30\;\mu\mathrm s,&S&=\frac{50}{30}\approx1.667\times.\end{aligned}A:TB:T​=10+max(10,30,12)=40μs,=10+max(20,18,12)=30μs,​SS​=4050​=1.25×,=3050​≈1.667×.​

A changes a noncritical term and does not improve the already-optimized 40 μs runtime. B removes the current bottleneck and exposes tensor time again. This is a resource lower-bound comparison; if dependencies prevent the assumed overlap, profile-based critical-path analysis is required.

Precision is a four-part contract

For any “FP8” or “FP4” result, specify: stored representation, multiply input representation, accumulation representation and final output representation. FP32 accumulation can reduce error from many small products, but it cannot restore information already lost by quantizing the operands. Scales may be per tensor, channel or small block; their loading and conversion can be a real part of the kernel. [39]

xi≈sx,gqx,i,wi≈sw,gqw,i,∑ixiwi≈∑gsx,gsw,g ⁣(∑i∈gqx,iqw,i),beffective=bpayload+bmetadata/groupG+btensor metadataN.\begin{aligned}x_i&\approx s_{x,g}q_{x,i},&w_i&\approx s_{w,g}q_{w,i},\\\sum_ix_iw_i&\approx\sum_gs_{x,g}s_{w,g}\!\left(\sum_{i\in g}q_{x,i}q_{w,i}\right),\\b_{\mathrm{effective}}&=b_{\mathrm{payload}}+\frac{b_{\mathrm{metadata/group}}}{G}+\frac{b_{\mathrm{tensor\ metadata}}}{N}.\end{aligned}xi​i∑​xi​wi​beffective​​≈sx,g​qx,i​,≈g∑​sx,g​sw,g​(i∈g∑​qx,i​qw,i​),=bpayload​+Gbmetadata/group​​+Nbtensor metadata​​.​wi​≈sw,g​qw,i​,

The scale product must be applied with the correct group boundaries and accumulation behavior. Smaller groups follow outliers more accurately but increase metadata and may require more scale operations. Weight-only INT4 often saves capacity and bandwidth while retaining higher-precision activations; FP4 tensor compute additionally requires a supported activation path. Neither should inherit the other's peak number.

Structured 2:4 sparsity is yet another contract: the allowed pattern must be enforced and encoded, and sparse matrix instructions must be used. Top-k MoE means different experts activate for different tokens; it does not mean each activated matrix satisfies 2:4 sparsity. Multiplying a sparse-FP4 peak by an MoE “sparsity factor” double-counts unrelated mechanisms.

Derivation: storage precision and accumulator precision enter different error terms

Assumptions. Consider a dot product z=Σᵢ₌₁ᴷxᵢwᵢ. Input quantization produces x̂ᵢ=xᵢ+eᵢ and ŵᵢ=wᵢ+δᵢ. Assume round-to-nearest, no overflow or underflow, and an accumulator with unit roundoff u. Scaled FP8/FP4 recipes violate a simple uniform relative-error model near zero or clipping, so retain explicit e and δ rather than pretending every format has the same u. See FP8 Formats for the format/scale distinction.

1. Expand the operand error before discussing accumulation.

∑ix^iw^i−∑ixiwi=∑i(eiwi+xiδi+eiδi),∣operand error∣≤∑i(∣ei∣∣wi∣+∣xi∣∣δi∣+∣ei∣∣δi∣).\begin{aligned}\sum_i\widehat x_i\widehat w_i-\sum_ix_iw_i&=\sum_i(e_iw_i+x_i\delta_i+e_i\delta_i),\\|\text{operand error}|&\le\sum_i\bigl(|e_i||w_i|+|x_i||\delta_i|+|e_i||\delta_i|\bigr).\end{aligned}i∑​xi​wi​−i∑​xi​wi​∣operand error∣​=i∑​(ei​wi​+xi​δi​+ei​δi​),≤i∑​(∣ei​∣∣wi​∣+∣xi​∣∣δi​∣+∣ei​∣∣δi​∣).​

The cross term is second order only when both errors are genuinely small. Saturation can make it material. If both inputs satisfy relative bounds |eᵢ|≤uₓ|xᵢ| and |δᵢ|≤u_w|wᵢ|, the operand bound simplifies to (uₓ+u_w+uₓu_w)Σ|xᵢwᵢ|. This is conditional on representability; block scaling and clipping determine whether the assumptions hold.

2. Add accumulator rounding. A standard sequential fused multiply-add model yields |fl(Σx̂ᵢŵᵢ)−Σx̂ᵢŵᵢ|≤γKΣ|x̂ᵢŵᵢ|, where γK=Ku/(1−Ku) and Ku<1. One way to see the factor is that each contribution is multiplied by a product of terms (1+εⱼ), |εⱼ|≤u; the deviation of at most K such factors is bounded by γK. Pairwise reductions, separate rounded multiplication, and special tensor-core accumulation rules change the appropriate bound.

3. Why FP32 accumulation does not restore FP16 operands. Wider accumulation reduces γK but cannot undo e or δ already introduced by operand conversion. Conversely, accurate inputs can still accumulate poorly in a narrow accumulator. For FP32 u≈2⁻²⁴ and K=4096, γK≈0.0002442. This is a worst-case absolute bound relative to the sum of product magnitudes, not a typical 0.024% relative output error: cancellation can make z tiny while Σ|xᵢwᵢ| stays large. Evaluate the numerical recipe as a complete multiply/accumulate/reduction path.

An alternative matrix organization: Gaudi and AMD chiplets

Gaudi 3 is useful for understanding a design with large matrix multiplication engines plus programmable tensor processors and integrated networking. The compiler divides matrix work among engines and tries to exploit operand reuse through the memory hierarchy. The source figure makes the partition explicit. [10]

The eight output regions correspond to two row partitions of A and four column partitions of B. An A row partition is reused by four engines; a B column partition is reused by two. If every engine independently fetched its operands from HBM, the mathematical partition would squander bandwidth. A cache/scratchpad and scheduler that maintain this reuse are therefore as important as the number of multiply-accumulate cells.

Contrast this with splitting K across engines: each produces a partial sum of the same output, so an extra reduction is required. Splitting M or N instead produces disjoint output tiles. These choices reappear in GPU split-K GEMM and distributed tensor parallelism. They change synchronization and memory traffic even when FLOPs are identical. Large arrays prefer substantial regular tiles, while many smaller engines can expose more scheduling flexibility; neither arrangement is inherently superior across all matrix shapes.

AMD CDNA 3 organizes compute and memory through chiplets and a large package-level memory system. Chiplets can improve yield and scale capacity, but the logical accelerator is not a physically uniform point. Placement, locality, cache policy and fabric traffic remain relevant inside the package. CDNA matrix instructions, wavefront execution and register resources differ from NVIDIA's; a CUDA-optimized tiling is not automatically an optimal ROCm kernel. [40]

The useful cross-vendor comparison is therefore not “same number of matrix units.” Compare achieved throughput on the model's exact GEMM shapes, the bytes read from external memory, conversion overhead, collective traces and the maturity of the selected runtime. A compiler can fuse normalization and projection differently on two machines, changing the workload before the hardware comparison even begins.

H100’s published BF16 tensor number of 1,979 TFLOP/s is marked with sparsity; the corresponding dense rate is approximately half. Larger HBM can improve performance discontinuously: it may eliminate a second device, avoid weight offload, admit a useful batch, or retain more KV cache. When a workload already fits comfortably, additional capacity by itself does not increase the speed of reading existing weights.

Custom datacenter accelerators

TPU: matrix arrays plus a topology-aware compiler

TPUs combine matrix engines, vector operations, scratchpad memory, and an inter-chip network. XLA and kernel scheduling determine how well operations map onto those resources. The relevant unit may be a chip, a slice, or a pod; a pod total cannot be compared directly with a single GPU.

The table is from Google’s TPU7x documentation. Ironwood’s FP8 figure is 4,614 TFLOP/s; substituting it for BF16 would create a twofold comparison error. [11]

The 2026 TPU 8t / 8i architecture split is instructive: 8t emphasizes training, with 216 GB HBM and 6,528 GB/s; 8i emphasizes serving, with 288 GB and 8,601 GB/s. Their disclosed SRAM capacities are 128 MB and 384 MB. The 8i design adds a collectives acceleration engine and Boardfly topology, while 8t uses a 3D torus. This is evidence that reducing communication delay and increasing memory resources can matter more for serving than maximizing one compute figure. These are official architecture specifications, not a matched public LLM result in our table. [12]

Trainium, Gaudi, and Ascend

Trainium2 provides 96 GiB memory at 2.9 TB/s, 667 dense BF16 TFLOP/s, and 1,299 FP8 TFLOP/s per chip. NeuronLink and dedicated collective engines connect chips; compilation and supported kernels are central to utilization. Trainium3 raises disclosed HBM to 144 GB and bandwidth to 4.9 TB/s per chip. An UltraServer aggregate must be divided by its chip count only when the per-chip interpretation is actually useful. [13] [14]

Gaudi 3 OAM has 128 GB HBM2e at 3.7 TB/s, 96 MB on-die SRAM, and a 900 W TDP reference. Integrated Ethernet changes the system design and collective implementation. Model coverage, software maturity, and operator support remain as important as capacity. [10]

Ascend deserves its own software and interconnect analysis. Huawei’s official roadmap connects the 910C-based Atlas 900 A3 SuperPoD with later 950 variants specialized for prefill/recommendation or decode/training. Do not transfer a 950 memory figure to 910C, or fill missing public chip specifications with unsourced estimates. The relevant practical questions are CANN operator support, HCCL communication, model conversion, and measured end-to-end throughput on the available system. [15]

SRAM-centric designs: bandwidth bought with a different system

Cerebras WSE-3 places 44 GB SRAM across a wafer with many compute cores. That memory is distributed next to computation; its aggregate internal bandwidth is not equivalent to one large uniform HBM port. Models beyond local capacity require a system-level mapping, streaming strategy, or multiple wafers. [16]

The August 2026 CS-4 announcement uses three WSE-3T wafers, each retaining 44 GB SRAM, with an advertised aggregate 129.6 PB/s memory bandwidth. The announcement reports over 4,400 tokens/s/user on GPT-OSS-120B under its own conditions. This is a vendor launch result; it cannot be ranked against our Llama2 MLPerf table. The useful architectural lesson is the trade between extremely fast local access, available storage, and multi-wafer distribution. [17]

Historical GroqChip documentation describes 230 MB SRAM and 80 TB/s on-chip bandwidth, with deterministic compiler scheduling across devices. A large model requires many chips, so low per-user latency does not by itself reveal rack cost or aggregate capacity. The 2026 Groq platform page describes a newer LPX direction; historical per-chip figures should not be relabeled as specifications for that future system. [18] [19]

Insight: SRAM-heavy and HBM-heavy systems allocate silicon and system resources differently. Compare equal models and output quality at equal latency targets, including total chips, power, and cost. “Bandwidth per chip” is particularly misleading when one chip is a wafer and another is a reticle-sized device.

SRAM-centric systems: read the capacity–bandwidth bargain

The attractive part of SRAM is access energy and bandwidth at a short physical distance. The expensive part is area per stored bit. Replacing HBM with on-chip SRAM consequently exchanges capacity for locality. For a model whose weights fit across a fast connected SRAM system, low-batch decode may avoid repeatedly streaming the same weights from external DRAM. If the weights do not fit, the design needs enough devices or an external streaming path, and the bottleneck moves to that path. [16] [18]

Distributed SRAM also has an ownership structure. A core's local memory cannot necessarily satisfy every other core at the same advertised rate. Mapping weights, activations and routes determines which network links carry traffic. Aggregate bandwidth sums many independent local accesses; it is attainable only if the workload supplies the right distributed access pattern. A wafer's aggregate PB/s number and a GPU's HBM TB/s number therefore describe different levels of the hierarchy.

Groq's historical tensor-streaming approach makes much of the schedule explicit in the compiler. Predictable operation timing can eliminate some dynamic arbitration and improve low-latency execution, but it increases the importance of compile-time mapping and supported shapes. Cerebras places a large number of cores and SRAM on a wafer with a mesh; the opportunity is extreme local parallelism and short communication, while the challenge is mapping a large model and its traffic onto that distributed fabric. These are distinct architectures despite both emphasizing SRAM.

A rigorous capacity comparison counts all chips required for weights plus runtime state, not only a model's active arithmetic. A sparse model still needs access to its total expert pool. A system can quote excellent per-user speed by spreading one request over a large number of chips; another can quote excellent aggregate throughput by batching many requests on fewer chips. Both may be valid operating points. To compare them, plot latency against delivered throughput at a fixed total system budget and quality.

When capacity savings buy less communication

Consider two options for the same model: two 80 GB GPUs or one 192 GB accelerator. If the second fits weights and KV with adequate headroom, it may avoid all per-layer inter-device reductions. Even with lower single-chip arithmetic peak, it can be faster at small batch. The comparison reverses when a compute-heavy prefill batch benefits enough from two devices. This is an architectural explanation for workload-dependent rankings, not a prediction about particular products.

Conversely, a large SRAM cluster can distribute weight reads broadly but still pay for activation exchange at every layer. A lower bound must include that network path, not only local memory access. The relevant metric is the critical-path service time for the mapped graph. The maximum of all local resource rates only describes throughput when independent work can keep those resources active.

Derivation: fitting a model can be worth more than a faster arithmetic peak

Set up two placements. A dense decoding step touches W weight bytes. A smaller accelerator retains Mᵣ bytes of those weights and must transfer D=max(0,W−Mᵣ) bytes from a slower tier each iteration; assume no useful cross-iteration retention for the missing portion. Let βoff be useful transfer bandwidth and tcomp the duration of independent compute available to overlap it. A larger device fits the weights but may have a slower local kernel. These assumptions deliberately isolate the capacity discontinuity described above.

1. Bound the smaller system's iteration. Even ideal scheduling must transfer D bytes, so the overlap-capable phase costs at least max(tcomp,D/βoff). If the transfer cannot start until the dependent stage, the cost is instead additive. A fast HBM rate cannot remove the separate slow-link bound.

Tsmall≥Tother+max⁡ ⁣(tcomp,Dβoff),Texposed≥max⁡ ⁣(0,Dβoff−tcomp),Full hiding requiresD≤βofftcomp.\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{small}}&\ge T_{\mathrm{other}}+\max\!\left(t_{\mathrm{comp}},\frac D{\beta_{\mathrm{off}}}\right),\\T_{\mathrm{exposed}}&\ge\max\!\left(0,\frac D{\beta_{\mathrm{off}}}-t_{\mathrm{comp}}\right),\\\text{Full hiding requires}\quad D&\le\beta_{\mathrm{off}}t_{\mathrm{comp}}.\end{aligned}Tsmall​Texposed​Full hiding requiresD​≥Tother​+max(tcomp​,βoff​D​),≥max(0,βoff​D​−tcomp​),≤βoff​tcomp​.​

2. Account for the prefetch buffer. Hiding transfer also requires storage for prefetched data before the current unit is freed. For unit size U, a two-unit schedule may need current U plus next U on top of persistent state. “It fits one unit” is not enough to establish that prefetch can work. If a transfer unit is smaller, startup cost becomes more important; if larger, live memory rises.

Example. Missing 6 GB of weights on a 32 GB/s useful host link gives a transfer floor of 187.5 ms per iteration. A 20 ms compute window can hide at most 0.64 GB, leaving at least 167.5 ms exposed under this simple model. A device that fits the model and takes 35 ms locally can be faster despite slower arithmetic. Offload still has value when it enables an otherwise impossible workload; feasibility and latency are different objectives. Actual heterogeneous systems can change residency, layer placement and batching, so use the transferred bytes of the measured schedule.

Exercise — How much offload can a prefetch window hide?

A layer unit is 0.8 GB, the useful transfer rate is 40 GB/s, and independent computation lasts 12 ms. Assume two buffers fit and ignore startup. What part of the transfer is exposed? What useful bandwidth would fully hide it?

Show worked solution
Ttransfer=0.840  s=20  ms,Texposed=max⁡(0,20−12)=8  ms,BWrequired=0.8  GB0.012  s≈66.67  GB/s.\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{transfer}}&=\frac{0.8}{40}\;\mathrm s=20\;\mathrm{ms},\\T_{\mathrm{exposed}}&=\max(0,20-12)=8\;\mathrm{ms},\\\mathrm{BW}_{\mathrm{required}}&=\frac{0.8\;\mathrm{GB}}{0.012\;\mathrm s}\approx66.67\;\mathrm{GB/s}.\end{aligned}Ttransfer​Texposed​BWrequired​​=400.8​s=20ms,=max(0,20−12)=8ms,=0.012s0.8GB​≈66.67GB/s.​

Two buffers remove a storage obstacle but do not change the link rate. The computed 8 ms is a best case; resource contention or a later-ready transfer can expose more time. A bandwidth specification should be replaced with the useful application rate when predicting the schedule.

How to use the Chinese-vendor entries

The seven represented vendors are Huawei, Alibaba/T-Head, Biren, Cambricon, Kunlunxin, MetaX, and Moore Threads. Disclosure is uneven: a product can be deployed while its die area, fabrication, or arithmetic table remains unavailable in the sources checked. NR is therefore an evidence boundary, not a judgment of competitiveness. Ascend roadmap figures retain their announcement vintage; they are not substituted for observed shipping-device measurements.

For newer product tracking, Moore Threads documents MTT S5000/PH100; Biren lists the 550 W 166M OAM; and MetaX lists C550/C588/C600 families. These names should not inherit older chips’ process, area, bandwidth, or compute numbers. Huawei’s September 2026 system announcement also updates its future platform direction; the historical 2025 950 rows above remain explicitly dated.

Why these special architectures need different comparisons

Programmability has several levels. A programmable GPU can accept new model weights and kernels. A spatial or streaming accelerator still supports programmable models, but mapping and scheduling constraints become central. Taalas goes further by hardwiring the base model; its reported support for LoRA and configurable context does not make replacing the base weights equivalent to loading a GPU checkpoint. Its 3-/6-bit quantization also changes output quality. The HC1 result is a vendor demonstration, with a product-chart sequence label of “1k/1k”; concurrency, server count, and energy methodology are not sufficiently specified there for a matched efficiency ranking. Taalas design statement.

SRAM capacity is a system constraint. With P parameters, q stored bits per parameter, per-device available weight memory C, and no weight streaming, a capacity-only lower bound is N≥⌈Pq8C⌉N\ge\left\lceil\frac{Pq}{8C}\right\rceilN≥⌈8CPq​⌉. For a hypothetical 70B model at 4 bits, weights alone occupy 35 GB. At 230 MB per historical GroqChip, this gives at least 153 chips even before scales, code, activations, KV, and placement constraints. This is a capacity illustration—not a prediction of Groq’s actual deployment. SRAM bandwidth cannot remove a capacity requirement.

Derive useful comparisons from the reference

For dense decode, let B be batch size, P parameter count, q weight bits, F arithmetic rate, and β weight-memory bandwidth. Reading each weight once per batch gives weight traffic Pq/8 and approximately 2PB operations. The arithmetic intensity is I≈16BqI\approx\frac{16B}{q}I≈q16B​ FLOP/byte. Equating compute and memory time gives B∗≈qF16βB^*\approx\frac{qF}{16\beta}B∗≈16βqF​. This is an idealized crossover that excludes attention, scales, unpacking, communication, and imperfect reuse; F must match the actual kernel’s arithmetic format.

Using dense BF16 weights and matrix peaks: MI300X gives B* ≈ (16 × 1.3×10¹⁵)/(16 × 5.3×10¹²) ≈ 245; MI355X gives ≈313 using its rounded 2.5 PF and 8 TB/s. Increasing compute faster than bandwidth raises the batch needed to reach the compute roof. It does not imply the newer chip is slower: both roofs and capacity must be compared at the workload’s batch and latency target.

For a link budget, if n full-duplex ports each carry r gigabits/s in each direction, the summed one-direction line rate is β=nr8\beta=\frac{nr}{8}β=8nr​ GB/s; summing both directions gives 2β. Protocol overhead, routing, simultaneous traffic, and topology reduce delivered bandwidth. On a graph, the traffic across a cut is constrained by the sum of the capacities of the links crossing that cut, regardless of the sum of all device links elsewhere.

Exercise: why can a “2× bandwidth” claim fail to halve latency?

Suppose 60% of baseline time is bandwidth-limited work improved exactly 2×, while 40% is unchanged. Then T′/T = 0.6/2 + 0.4 = 0.7, so speedup is 1/0.7 ≈ 1.43×. If the faster component creates more network contention, even this assumes too much. Validate the new bottleneck, rather than applying bandwidth ratios to complete LLM latency.

Exercise: normalize the B300 HGX FP4 figure

The cited HGX table lists 144 PF sparse and 108 PF dense for eight GPUs. Dense per GPU is 108/8 = 13.5 PF. Dividing 144 by 8 and then by 2 gives 9 PF, which is wrong for this entry: the table explicitly supplies a different dense value. Read each footnote before applying a generic sparsity multiplier.

Reference workflow: select the exact SKU and date; check model fit and supported arithmetic; derive the likely memory/compute/communication roof; then use the measured benchmark sections below. A launch claim or peak specification never fills a missing matched-model benchmark.

Reading a price sheet correctly

DigitalOcean's cited rates took effect August 1, 2026. Its spot instances are reclaimable; powered-off allocated GPU instances remain billable until destroyed. A low reserved rate still incurs a contractual commitment. Lambda's cited prices are per GPU-hour, so an eight-GPU booking costs eight times that rate, plus applicable taxes. These examples explain why a bare “$/hour” column is insufficient.

For Chinese accelerators, obtain the exact board revision, accelerator count, host memory, interconnect, software/support term, delivery date and VAT treatment in CNY. For wafer-scale or SRAM-centric systems, also request the minimum viable cluster for your model. This reference does not fill gaps with unsourced marketplace asking prices or divide a cluster procurement total by chip count when the other components are unknown.

An NPU’s TOPS number does not tell you whether a particular attention layout, KV representation, or dynamic shape runs efficiently. Unsupported operators can fall back to CPU/GPU and add transfers. A model fitting in unified memory can be useful even if generation is slower than on a discrete GPU; a discrete GPU that cannot hold it may require expensive offload.

For an edge robot, camera pipelines and perception compete with policy inference. Measure sustained performance at the allowed power and ambient temperature. A short benchmark before thermal equilibrium can overstate usable throughput. The Orin study explicitly varies batch, sequence length, quantization, and power, and finds that low-bit execution is not always faster for smaller models. [31]

Edge hardware in depth: bandwidth, kernels, and energy interact

The RTX Blackwell SM diagram exposes the resources that an LLM kernel shares. Register files hold thread-local values and accumulators; shared memory supports cooperative tiling; schedulers issue instructions to several execution units. The graphics-oriented RT core is visible because this is a consumer GPU architecture. Its presence does not make ray-tracing throughput a useful LLM metric. Even within the same architecture family, consumer and datacenter chips differ in memory interface, capacity, interconnect and sometimes supported instruction details. [21]

Unified memory removes copies, not contention

A unified CPU/GPU memory system can avoid a separate host-to-device copy and permit large model residency. It does not create infinite bandwidth or exclusive GPU ownership. The CPU, GPU, display, camera pipelines and other accelerators may share memory controllers. Runtime memory reservations and operating-system pressure reduce usable capacity. On a discrete GPU, dedicated memory is easier to isolate, but a model spilling over PCIe pays a much larger transfer penalty.

On an NPU, graph compilation may require a supported set of quantized operators and static or bounded shapes. An unsupported attention or sampling operation can split the graph into accelerator and CPU segments. Boundary tensors then incur synchronization and possible layout conversion. The correct performance unit is the full graph, including fallback, rather than the subgraph whose TOPS utilization is high. Dynamic KV cache growth can be especially awkward for a compiler designed around fixed vision tensors.

Why quantization can make a small model slower

The Orin study uses a Jetson AGX Orin 64 GB, JetPack 6.0, CUDA 12.2, PyTorch 2.3.0 and Transformers, and evaluates BitsAndBytes-based lower-precision paths. Its graph shows that FP16 can outperform INT8/INT4 for some smaller models while low precision enables larger models to fit. The mechanism is plausible: dequantization, scale handling, unfavorable GEMM shapes and insufficiently optimized kernels can cost more than the bytes saved. This should not be generalized to every INT4 kernel on Orin. A different fused kernel or batch regime can change the result. [31]

Read the y-axis carefully: this study's throughput counts input plus output tokens divided by total batch latency. That is not output-only generation speed. Its default short workload includes 32 input and 64 generated tokens; comparing the plotted number directly with a vendor's output tokens/s would favor a different numerator. The paper also reports memory and latency on separate axes: smaller memory footprint does not imply lower latency. These are valuable results precisely because they separate the three outcomes.

Quantization experiments should preserve the exact model, tokenizer, sampling settings, prompt/output lengths and quality evaluation. Report both storage bits and execution path. If a lower-bit model permits a larger batch, show one comparison at equal batch and another at each configuration's capacity-limited optimum. The first isolates kernel/representation effects; the second measures deployable throughput. Mixing them conceals why the result changed.

Energy is the integral, not the lowest power reading

Power modes vary different clock domains. In the source, A/B reduce GPU clocks, C/D CPU clocks, E/F active CPU cores, and G/H memory clocks. Severe memory-clock reduction can cause a large latency increase even though instantaneous power falls. A memory-limited model may tolerate a modest core-clock reduction much better than a memory-clock reduction. This offers a targeted optimization strategy: reduce a resource with slack, rather than lowering every clock together.

Erequest=∫0TrequestPsystem(t) dt,Etoken=ErequestNuseful output,Psystem≈Pstatic+Pmemory+Pcompute+PCPU+Pother.\begin{aligned}E_{\mathrm{request}}&=\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{request}}}P_{\mathrm{system}}(t)\,dt,\\E_{\mathrm{token}}&=\frac{E_{\mathrm{request}}}{N_{\mathrm{useful\ output}}},\\P_{\mathrm{system}}&\approx P_{\mathrm{static}}+P_{\mathrm{memory}}+P_{\mathrm{compute}}+P_{\mathrm{CPU}}+P_{\mathrm{other}}.\end{aligned}Erequest​Etoken​Psystem​​=∫0Trequest​​Psystem​(t)dt,=Nuseful output​Erequest​​,≈Pstatic​+Pmemory​+Pcompute​+PCPU​+Pother​.​

For a hypothetical request, 30 W for 10 s consumes 300 J; 20 W for 20 s consumes 400 J. The lower power setting is less energy-efficient in that case. Conversely, racing to completion can waste energy if voltage/frequency increases add much more power than they save time. Measure the curve rather than assume either policy wins.

Robotic edge deployments introduce deadline and coexistence constraints. A language or action model sharing memory bandwidth with video processing may miss deadlines even when standalone average throughput looks adequate. Include sensor acquisition, preprocessing, control output and thermal steady state in the experiment. If a system has a 50 ms action deadline, a high-throughput batch that completes every 500 ms is not an equivalent solution.

Derivation: an energy-optimal frequency depends on whether time still decreases

Illustrative model. Suppose a compute-bound request requires C clock cycles, runs at frequency f, and takes T=C/f. Approximate power by P(f)=P₀+af³: P₀ is frequency-independent system power and the cubic term represents a simplified voltage/frequency-dependent dynamic cost. This is an analytical toy model, not a universal device power law. The edge study measures why clocks and energy must be considered together.

1. Energy has a time term as well as a power term.

E(f)=P(f)T(f)=(P0+af3)Cf=P0Cf+aCf2,dEdf=−P0Cf2+2aCf,f∗=(P02a)1/3.\begin{aligned}E(f)&=P(f)T(f)=(P_0+af^3)\frac Cf\\&=\frac{P_0C}{f}+aCf^2,\\\frac{dE}{df}&=-\frac{P_0C}{f^2}+2aCf,\\f^*&=\left(\frac{P_0}{2a}\right)^{1/3}.\end{aligned}E(f)dfdE​f∗​=P(f)T(f)=(P0​+af3)fC​=fP0​C​+aCf2,=−f2P0​C​+2aCf,=(2aP0​​)1/3.​

The second derivative 2P₀C/f³+2aC is positive, so the point is the unique minimum inside the valid frequency range. Reducing frequency below f* spends too long paying static power; increasing it above f* spends too much on dynamic power. A latency deadline τ additionally requires f≥C/τ, so the feasible optimum is the unconstrained optimum projected onto the device's frequency limits and that deadline.

2. The bandwidth-bound case changes the derivative. If time is instead fixed by data transfer T≈D/β over some frequency interval, E≈(P₀+af³)D/β grows with f in that interval. Raising compute frequency cannot improve that fixed bottleneck, so it only increases energy in this model. In a combined model T=max(C/f,D/β), the crossover frequency is f_cross=Cβ/D, and the energy curve must be analyzed on both sides.

Example. Measure f in GHz, choose P₀=20 W, a=5 W/GHz³ and C=10 billion cycles. Then f*=2^(1/3)≈1.260 GHz and E(f*)≈238.1 J. At 1 GHz, E=250 J; at 2 GHz, E=300 J. The fastest setting is not the energy minimum, but a 5-second deadline forces f≥2 GHz and changes the choice. Wall power, thermal throttling, memory clocks and idle policy must be measured for a real system.
