Only 2 GHz meets the deadline. An energy-only comparison would choose a slower point, but the constrained problem chooses the lowest energy among points that satisfy latency. Real DVFS policies also need margin for variability and should use measured energy at each available clock state.

Worked design exercise: choose resources from the workload

Case A: interactive dense decode with a model that fits

Begin with weight bytes, then add KV for the expected context distribution. Profile the actual quantized linear kernels at batch 1, 2, 4 and 8. If latency is near the weight-bandwidth lower bound, more matrix arithmetic will do little; improve achieved bandwidth, reduce bytes or increase reuse within the latency budget. If measured time is several times the bound, inspect launches, dequantization, tensor shapes and fallback before buying more bandwidth.

For 8B parameters at 4.5 bits, the 4.5 GB weight stream at a measured 200 GB/s takes at least 22.5 ms. That is a 44.4 output-token/s weight-only ceiling. Add a 16K-token GQA cache under the earlier 128 KiB/token model and another 2 GiB must be read per batch-one step in the pessimistic streaming model. The total bandwidth lower bound is about 33.2 ms before scalar work and launches. The computation explicitly shows why a context-length benchmark is necessary.

Case B: compute-heavy prompt processing

For T prompt tokens, dense linear work is roughly 2PT forward FLOPs. Exact attention adds a term quadratic in prompt length, with causal masking changing the useful arithmetic count. A large prompt often supplies enough rows for efficient GEMM, but long attention can shift the bottleneck to the attention kernel's internal resources. Measure time by layer category; do not assign the whole prefill phase to a single dense-GEMM roofline.

Lower precision may improve this phase if the activation/weight kernel supports faster instructions and quality remains acceptable. Tensor parallelism can reduce compute latency if its reductions stay on a sufficiently fast fabric. At higher request rates, separate replicas may deliver better cost or queueing behavior than a larger TP group. Splitwise's central hardware insight is that prefill and generation need not use identical resources, provided the KV transfer earns its cost. [38]

Case C: long-context, many-request serving

Here capacity limits admitted requests and KV traffic grows with both batch and context. Prefix reuse, GQA/MLA and cache quantization can change the hardware requirement more than a chip generation. When comparing two chips, first fix whether they use identical cache representations and prefix-hit rates. A benchmark with a warm shared prefix is a different service than one with independent long prompts.

If the working set does not fit in HBM, distinguish active KV from reusable inactive prefixes. Restoring a prefix once can be profitable; reading a remote history on every generated token can saturate the link. The measured useful throughput depends on the cache manager and storage hierarchy, so HBM capacity and a fast network should be evaluated together. The KV cache guide develops that admission and placement problem.

Case D: sparse expert inference

MoE lowers active arithmetic per token without proportionally lowering total weight storage. At small batches, selected experts may each receive too few rows for efficient tensor-core use. At larger batches, more of the expert pool becomes active, increasing the working set and all-to-all traffic. Compare routed-token histograms, grouped-GEMM efficiency and network exposure, not only active parameter count. A high-HBM-capacity accelerator may enable local expert placement and remove a network transfer that a smaller chip requires.

Case E: training at cluster scale

Training adds gradients, optimizer states and stored/recomputed activations. Its useful objective is target quality per time or cost, so a lower-precision path that requires extra steps must be evaluated at convergence. Once a model is partitioned, network topology and overlap can dominate scaling efficiency. A chip with excellent local throughput may produce poor cluster throughput when all-gather and all-reduce repeatedly cross a congested fabric. Consult the distributed guide before extrapolating single-device TFLOP/s to a large training system.

For these selected submissions, B300’s Server throughput is about 7.0% above MI355X’s; B200’s Offline throughput is about 0.46% above MI355X’s. Those are derived system-result ratios. They do not isolate silicon effects: host, kernels, parallelism, clocks, quantization recipe, and runtime differ. A sub-percent difference is particularly poor evidence for a broad architecture ranking. The FP8 and FP4 groups also differ in representation.

The benchmark extract is saved with this library as hardware_benchmark_evidence.json, including IDs, software strings, and source locations. This is a reproducible selection rather than an exhaustive best-result leaderboard. Results without comparable public entries are left unranked.

Measured edge results: read the concurrency label

NVIDIA’s Thor developer-kit page reports the following output throughput using input/output lengths 2,048/128 and its described JetPack 7.0, CUDA 13.0, TensorRT 10.13 environment; LLM/VLM runs use vLLM. The summary does not specify every precision and accuracy detail, so these figures should remain within this table’s context. [30]

Model on the same AGX ThorMax concurrency 1Max concurrency 8
Llama 3.1 8B41.3 tokens/s150.8 tokens/s
Llama 3.3 70B4.7 tokens/s12.6 tokens/s
Qwen3 30B-A3B61.0 tokens/s226.4 tokens/s

The higher concurrency figure is aggregate throughput. Dividing by eight gives a rough throughput share only if eight requests remain continuously active; it is not the measured latency of each request. Qwen’s sparse A3B model and dense 32B model have different work per token, so comparing them illustrates architecture effects as well as hardware behavior.

Total cost of ownership: derive cost per useful result

TCO connects chip architecture to economics. The objective is to deliver a specified workload and quality within a latency or completion-time constraint at minimum lifetime cost.

1. Fix the comparison boundary

Specify model/version, precision and quality, input/output length distribution, context-cache hit rate, concurrency, TTFT/TPOT limits, and required availability. Measure aggregate throughput of the whole priced system. Single-user token speed, peak FLOPS and aggregate serving throughput are different quantities. For training, use cost to reach the same validation target, including failed runs, restarts and data preparation.

2. Build the cost numerator without double counting

CTCO=C0−V+∑y=1Y(Ey+Oy)C_{\mathrm{TCO}}=C_0-V+\sum_{y=1}^Y(E_y+O_y)CTCO​=C0​−V+y=1∑Y​(Ey​+Oy​)

C0 is installed capital: accelerators, CPU/DRAM, NICs, switches, storage, racks, installation and your allocated facility investment. V is residual value at the end of Y years. O includes support, licenses, labor, repairs, recurring network/storage and facility charges. Include only costs inside the chosen boundary, allocating shared infrastructure consistently. Do not add depreciation to this cash-flow sum: it would count the purchase twice. Conversely, an amortized annual analysis replaces the purchase with its annual charge.

Let PL and PI be measured whole-system loaded and idle power in kW, a the fraction of calendar time in the loaded state, e the electricity tariff per kWh, and PUE the ratio of facility energy to IT energy. In a simplified continuously powered two-state model:

P‾IT=aPL+(1−a)PI,Eannual=8760 P‾IT PUE e.\begin{aligned}\overline P_{\mathrm{IT}}&=aP_L+(1-a)P_I,\\E_{\mathrm{annual}}&=8760\,\overline P_{\mathrm{IT}}\,\mathrm{PUE}\,e.\end{aligned}PIT​Eannual​​=aPL​+(1−a)PI​,=8760PIT​PUEe.​

This is an approximation to integrating power over time, E = ∫ e(t)Pfacility(t)dt. Use measured multi-state traces when load varies; account separately for demand charges or time-varying tariffs. If cooling electricity is already included through PUE, do not add it again. Facility rent and cooling equipment capital can still be separate costs. Chip TDP alone omits host, memory, networking and power-conversion losses. The Green Grid: PUE definition and measurement.

3. Derive the useful-work denominator

Let A be operational availability, u the fraction of available time doing productive work at the measured rate, and R the sustained useful output-token rate while doing that work. R must satisfy the latency and quality contract and include the cost of processing the associated prompts. It is aggregate system throughput, not token speed for one stream. With constant workload and performance:

Tproductive=8760YAuhours,Nout=3600 TproductiveR,cmillion=106CTCONout.\begin{aligned}T_{\mathrm{productive}}&=8760YAu\quad\text{hours},\\N_{\mathrm{out}}&=3600\,T_{\mathrm{productive}}R,\\c_{\mathrm{million}}&=\frac{10^6C_{\mathrm{TCO}}}{N_{\mathrm{out}}}.\end{aligned}Tproductive​Nout​cmillion​​=8760YAuhours,=3600Tproductive​R,=Nout​106CTCO​​.​

A and u factor calendar-time losses; R captures performance during productive intervals. Do not multiply by “GPU utilization” again if its effect is already in measured R. Rejected speculative tokens, failed requests and internal retries are not useful outputs. Either exclude them when measuring R or adjust the denominator explicitly, once. The power fraction a can exceed Au because booting, warming, failed work and background jobs consume power without useful output.

In general use N = ∫Ruseful(t)dt instead of a constant rate. Input and output tokens have different costs. The scalar above attributes all costs to output tokens for a fixed prompt/output mix; it is not a universal API rate. For an API bill, C = pinNin/10⁶ + poutNout/10⁶, adding cached-input, tool and storage charges as applicable. For agents, cost per successfully completed task is often more useful than cost per token.

4. Worked example: more expensive hardware can be cheaper per token

Synthetic assumptions, not vendor quotations or benchmark results. Both systems serve the same workload and quality under the same SLO. Y = 3 years, V = 0, A = 0.98, u = a = 0.50, PUE = 1.2, e = USD 0.10/kWh, and non-energy operating cost is USD 30,000/year.

QuantitySystem ASystem B
Installed capitalUSD 200,000USD 300,000
Loaded / idle power5 / 2 kW8 / 3 kW
SLO-compliant output R2,000 token/s4,000 token/s
Annual energy costUSD 3,679.20USD 5,781.60
Three-year TCOUSD 301,037.60USD 407,344.80
Useful output92.71584 billion tokens185.43168 billion tokens
Cost / million output tokensUSD 3.247USD 2.197

B costs about 35% more over its life but produces twice the useful work in this scenario, reducing cost per token by about 32%. This conclusion depends on having enough demand. If B's productive utilization falls to 25%, its output advantage disappears. Holding B's power assumptions fixed would raise its cost to USD 4.393/million; reducing its loaded power fraction to 25% lowers that only to approximately USD 4.351/million.

5. Architecture changes the economic denominator

  • Memory capacity: crossing a model-plus-KV capacity threshold can eliminate an entire model-parallel node. This changes capital, network traffic and useful throughput discontinuously.
  • Memory bandwidth: improves low-batch decode only while bandwidth is the bottleneck. If demand is low, faster completion need not create more billable work on an always-on owned system.
  • Interconnect: expensive scale-up fabrics can pay back by increasing delivered throughput or reducing synchronization time; count switches and power in the same system boundary.
  • Precision: lower bits can reduce both capacity and bandwidth cost, but only compare quality-validated workloads. Conversion, calibration and kernel engineering are part of deployment cost.
  • Specialized chips: include model compilation, porting, minimum cluster size and utilization across your model portfolio. Very high speed on one fixed model may not translate to economical heterogeneous demand.

For equal Y and workload, system B wins on token cost precisely when:

RBRA>CBCAAAuAABuB\frac{R_B}{R_A}>\frac{C_B}{C_A}\frac{A_Au_A}{A_Bu_B}RA​RB​​>CA​CB​​AB​uB​AA​uA​​

This follows by cross-multiplying CB/(ABuBRB) < CA/(AAuARA). It is a more useful purchase criterion than FLOPS per dollar.

6. Owning versus renting: derive a break-even point

Assume equal capacity and useful throughput. Let K be annual fixed ownership cost including amortized capital, staff and always-on idle electricity; v incremental electricity/operating cost per active system-hour above that idle baseline; p cloud price per allocated whole-system hour; and h productive hours/year. If cloud allocation exactly tracks productive hours:

Cown=K+vh,Ccloud=ph,h∗=Kp−vprovided p>v.\begin{aligned}C_{\mathrm{own}}&=K+vh,&C_{\mathrm{cloud}}&=ph,\\h^*&=\frac K{p-v}\quad\text{provided }p>v.\end{aligned}Cown​h∗​=K+vh,=p−vK​provided p>v.​Ccloud​=ph,

For synthetic K = USD 80,000/year, v = USD 1/hour and p = USD 32/hour, h* ≈ 2,581 hours/year, or 29.5% of calendar time. If cloud allocation is β times productive time due to idle bookings/warm-up, replace p by βp. Add cloud fixed costs to its side before solving. A reserved contract may charge all year regardless of h. If h* exceeds feasible productive hours, owning cannot win under these assumptions. Differences in availability, deployment speed, required redundancy or useful throughput invalidate a direct hourly comparison.

7. Capital cost, uncertainty and training

For a discounted annual analysis with cost of capital r, first remove the present value of resale, Cnet = C0 − V/(1+r)Y, then annualize it:

CRF⁡(r,Y)=r(1+r)Y(1+r)Y−1,Ccapital,annual=CnetCRF⁡(r,Y),lim⁡r→0CRF⁡(r,Y)=1Y.\begin{aligned}\operatorname{CRF}(r,Y)&=\frac{r(1+r)^Y}{(1+r)^Y-1},\\C_{\mathrm{capital,annual}}&=C_{\mathrm{net}}\operatorname{CRF}(r,Y),\\\lim_{r\to0}\operatorname{CRF}(r,Y)&=\frac1Y.\end{aligned}CRF(r,Y)Ccapital,annual​r→0lim​CRF(r,Y)​=(1+r)Y−1r(1+r)Y​,=Cnet​CRF(r,Y),=Y1​.​

Add annual operating costs to this charge. This is an alternative to the undiscounted calculator below; do not combine both capital charges. Model taxes, inflation and financing consistently when doing an investment analysis. Hardware obsolescence primarily changes the economically useful life, residual value and achievable utilization.

For training, if F is useful training FLOPs to reach a fixed target, P the cluster peak at the actual precision and η effective compute efficiency, compute time is approximately F/(ηP). Add checkpoint, evaluation and restart time not already captured in η. Multiply total allocated time by the cluster hourly cost, then include experiment failures and porting. A faster chip is economically useful only if it reduces cost to the same outcome or meets a valuable deadline.

Report a sensitivity grid over useful utilization, SLO throughput, capital price, lifetime and electricity cost. Holding the numerator fixed, halving u doubles token cost. Holding output fixed, a 10% energy reduction only reduces total cost by 10% times the energy share. For system A above, electricity is about 3.67% of TCO, so that saving is just 0.367% of total cost. Power can still be the decisive constraint when the site has a fixed MW budget.

8. Interactive ownership calculator

Defaults reproduce system A. All values describe a complete deployment; power is kW, money is USD. This is an undiscounted constant-workload scenario, not a vendor performance prediction.

Exercise: how much extra capital can a faster system justify?

At equal availability/utilization and 1.5× throughput, B needs total lifetime cost less than 1.5× A. If A costs USD 300,000 over its life, B's ceiling is USD 450,000. If B has USD 120,000 operating cost and zero residual value, its installed capital must be below USD 330,000. This assumes demand can consume the additional throughput.

Exercise: why can a cheaper spot rate lose?

Suppose a spot system costs USD 20/allocated hour and an uninterrupted one USD 30/hour at the same useful rate. If interruptions and recovery leave spot with productive fraction f, its effective price is 20/f per productive hour. It wins only when f > 2/3. Checkpoint storage and deadline penalties shift that threshold; an average saving does not guarantee completion by a fixed deadline.

Exercise: sensitivity to utilization versus power

Using system A, lower u from 50% to 25% while leaving all costs fixed. Output halves and cost rises from about USD 3.247 to 6.494/million. By contrast, lowering both power states by 20% saves USD 2,207.52 over three years and reduces cost to about USD 3.223/million. The relative importance changes with tariff, lifetime, hardware price and demand.

How to choose and measure a system

First fix the model, accuracy target, input/output length distribution, concurrency, and latency SLO. Specify whether prefix reuse, speculative decoding, quantization, and cached prompts are allowed. Include tokenizer and scheduler overhead when they are part of the user path.

Then measure a load sweep. Record p50/p95/p99 TTFT and output-token latency, successful request throughput, GPU memory high-water mark, utilization, and actual wall power. Include warmup and steady-state duration. Record exact model revision, runtime commit, kernel flags, parallelism, clocks, and power limits.

Goodput=completed requests meeting quality and latency targetssecond,Eaccepted token=measured system joulesaccepted output tokens,Cmillion=Csystem/hour×1063600 Ruseful tokens/s.\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Goodput}&=\frac{\text{completed requests meeting quality and latency targets}}{\text{second}},\\E_{\mathrm{accepted\ token}}&=\frac{\text{measured system joules}}{\text{accepted output tokens}},\\C_{\mathrm{million}}&=\frac{C_{\mathrm{system/hour}}\times10^6}{3600\,R_{\mathrm{useful\ tokens/s}}}.\end{aligned}GoodputEaccepted token​Cmillion​​=secondcompleted requests meeting quality and latency targets​,=accepted output tokensmeasured system joules​,=3600Ruseful tokens/s​Csystem/hour​×106​.​

A throughput maximum with poor latency can be unattractive for chat. A low-batch latency record can be unattractive for offline batch processing. Prefill/decode disaggregation can use different hardware for each phase, but the KV transfer and extra scheduling must earn their cost.

Workload-specific conclusions

  • Large-batch prefill and training: prioritize supported dense/low-precision matrix throughput, memory for activations, and efficient collectives.
  • Single-stream dense decode: prioritize achieved memory bandwidth and launch overhead after model fit is secured.
  • Long-context serving: prioritize KV capacity, attention kernels, and bandwidth; extra FLOPs alone may leave the bottleneck unchanged.
  • MoE serving: prioritize enough total weight capacity, grouped GEMM efficiency, and expert communication at the actual batch size.
  • Local experimentation: choose capacity and supported software first; estimate the bandwidth ceiling to set realistic expectations.
  • Battery or robotic edge: optimize task success within power, thermal, and response-time constraints, including concurrent perception workloads.

What a professional benchmark report must make reconstructible

A result should identify the exact model revision and tensor shapes, not merely “70B.” Record GQA/MQA/MLA configuration, context-length distribution, output-length cap, weight/KV formats including scales, target accuracy and whether speculative decoding is used. Input caching, prefix reuse and prompt construction change the amount of work. A token is not a universal unit of semantic information across tokenizers, so cross-model tokens/s is only a limited engineering comparison.

At the system level, record accelerator SKU, usable memory, host configuration, number of NICs, topology, power limit, clocks, runtime and kernel commits. A result using H200 NVL is not automatically representative of H200 SXM. An eight-device rack-level number cannot be divided by eight and treated as the performance of an independent single device when tensor parallelism and batching couple their execution.

For online serving, publish the load curve: requests per second against p50/p95/p99 TTFT and output-token latency, along with error rate and SLO attainment. A single maximum-throughput point hides how sharply the system approaches saturation. For offline serving, record total completion time and exact work quantity. For training, publish time to the quality target, loss curve, optimizer settings, total tokens and effective hardware utilization. Step time alone can reward a method that changes the optimization problem unfavorably.

For power, separate board telemetry from wall power and state whether CPUs, switches, cooling and idle infrastructure are included. Report measurement duration, sampling rate and thermal steady state. For cost, distinguish actual purchase/cloud prices from modeled assumptions. Capital amortization, utilization and availability affect delivered cost more than a simple purchase-price/FLOP ratio suggests.

A practical evidence hierarchy

EvidenceEstablishesDoes not establish
Datasheet or ISASupported capabilities and advertised limitsSustained model performance
MicrobenchmarkA resource rate or kernel shape under controlled conditionsEnd-to-end service quality
Matched model benchmarkPerformance for that model, runtime and workloadUniversal architecture superiority
Load sweep with SLOsCapacity of the service at defined latency and qualityLong-term reliability or economics by itself
Repeated production traceBehavior under realistic demand and operational effectsCausal attribution to one chip feature without an ablation

The most useful architecture papers connect levels of this hierarchy: a changed dataflow lowers a measured bottleneck, which then improves an end-to-end result. The figures in the historical chapters were chosen for that reason. A floor plan explains resource allocation; a scheduling diagram explains overlap; a roofline identifies a limit; a performance curve tests whether the limit moved.

Reading path and durable insights

Read roofline analysis and FlashAttention before product sheets. Then compare H100/H200 and MI300/MI325 to see how memory changes affect a similar compute family. Compare TPU 8t/8i to study workload specialization. Study SRAM-centric architectures as a different balance of storage, bandwidth, and system scale. Finally inspect benchmark submissions and reproduce one workload on the hardware you can access.

The durable lesson is that hardware and serving policy are coupled. Better batching can change which chip looks best. Quantization can reduce weight traffic but expose KV or communication costs. More memory can avoid an entire distributed execution boundary. A careful comparison explains these changes instead of treating every token/s figure as the same experiment.
